test.title: Bringing a bog back to life

paragraphs.text: Peat bogs cover only a small part of the Earth’s land surface, but they store more carbon than all the world’s forests combined. They form over thousands of years as dead plants build up in waterlogged ground, where there is too little oxygen for them to decay completely.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: In the past, many bogs were drained so that the land could be used for farming or so that peat could be cut and burned as fuel. Once a bog dries out, the stored carbon begins to escape into the atmosphere.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Restoration usually starts with blocking the drainage ditches using small dams made of peat or wood. As the water level rises, mosses return, and over time they begin to form new peat. On one restored site, the water table rose by 30 centimetres within two years.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Progress is slow, and results depend on the weather. A dry summer can undo much of the work, which is why restoration teams monitor water levels throughout the year and repair dams after heavy storms.
paragraphs.label: D
